raw_comment: To me, this graph really shows the power of empowerment. Over time, we have gotten much closer to attaining equal rights with men and have broken barriers that women back in the 1900s would never have deemed possible. This empowerment has allowed women to attain success in all fields of life, clearly even in running. The running times of women from the early 2000s to now have gotten much smaller and continue to decrease showing the evident capability and strength women have. However, this capability and strength only shines through when women are given the safe space to excel. We continue to get better at that as a society and for that I am proud.

raw_comment:
What I noticed, that over the span of the 2000s (when they started collecting the data) women have started getting faster. The dots have steadily increased upwards at a semi-constant rate, there were some outliers but for the most part, the dots were all bunched together.  

What I wonder, I wonder why women keep getting faster? Is it because of evolution? Are these women's bodies adapting and getting better traits to run like longer legs/slimmer bodies? And if so are only certain women evolving are those are the ones that are runners.

What impact this has on me and my community, well as a woman and as a woman that has women in my community this could be a great thing for us. People could look at this and start taking women runners more seriously and not put them down because of them being women. This could encourage women in my community to take running seriously if there passionate about it.

A catchy headline would be, women of the world speeding up will they slow down?

It looks like the graph goes up towards the end of the graph, and you can see an increase.  Some dots do not follow this increasing theme, but they all mostly increase in a line. I wonder how the speeds are getting much faster as time goes by and how the first speeds are so low compared to the new ones. As they're getting faster, who's competing against them?  "There has not been a large increase in the number of women who run marathons, yet the finishing times of the top 50 women finishers is getting faster."
"Of the 450 qualifying runners in the trials, two-thirds responded to the New York Times survey."

raw_comment:
I see that the graph goes up towards the end of the graph, and has a visible increase.  Some dots do not follow this increasing theme, but they all mostly increase in a line. I wonder how the speeds are getting much faster as time goes by and how the first speeds are so low compared to the new ones. As they're getting faster, who's competing against them? A good title that would fit this graph would be, "Speeding Women Getting Faster and Faster". My overall thoughts were that the speed's would not get that much faster over time. After seeing the graph more and reading the reveal, I realize that the speed increased a lot more than expected. 

3 Facts I found interesting from Reveal:  "Over the past 20 years, the time of the slowest of the top 50 women’s marathoners has decreased from about 2:50 hours to 2:35 hours."

 "There has not been a large increase in the number of women who run marathons, yet the finishing times of the top 50 women finishers is getting faster."

"Of the 450 qualifying runners in the trials, two-thirds responded to the New York Times survey."

What have I noticed? 
-This is a scatter plot graph
-As you go up the y-axis, the lengths of the marathons decrease.
-Over time, the lengths of these marathons became shorter

What do I wonder?
-Are the dots recorded gathered from the fastest, slowest, or average time it took to finish the race?
-If the marathon lengths were kept the same, would it show that the runners became faster?
-Why are the marathons becoming shorter over time?

What impact will it have on me or my community?
-Well the only thing I have in mind is that due to the decrease in the lengths of the marathons, it might provide less morale for the runners. A longer distance means more challenge, sparking intrigue in others. However, if you shorten it, there might not be as much interest.

raw_comment:
"Runner's High-Female Marathoner Edition" 
As I look over the data that this graph is displaying, I notice that every couple years, the average marathon time for a woman improves about one to two minutes. This makes me wonder what causes this improvement...does their training change in terms of difficulty? Do they eat or drink something different during the race itself? We may never know the answer, unless we ask these female athletes. Growing up in a family of runners, including myself, I tend to follow in my family's footsteps when it comes to training, eating+sleeping habits, etc. Beyond that, my family has seen great success in this sport, which makes me curious to what point are these women changing their running-related rituals to gain such impressive times. Do they run 3 workouts a week, rather than 2 workouts a week? Do they snack before a run or workout? Again, going back to my previous comment, we will only know the answers if we ask the athlete experiencing the improvements.

raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the graphs:  "Was That the Flash or a Women Running the 26.2 Mile Dash?" by CB4 of California, "Going Going Gone: Womens Marathon Running is Picking up the Pace!” by Libby J of New Hampshire, and "Woman Marathon Runners Just Keep Getting Faster!" by Phoebe of Humboldt County, California.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back tomorrow --  Thursday afternoon, September 24 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs) or 
a slide show of 60 of our favorite graphs (tinyurl.com/NYT60Graphs).  
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who is a fast walker but not a marathoner,  and Chris Adkisson of Somerset, Kentucky, who lazily prefers a good Gilmore Girls marathon!

raw_comment:
We noticed that the fastest 50 US women’s marathoners are faster than ever before. We see that the graph is a positive correlation and the slowest runner is still faster than another other runner in previous years. However, We do notice the highest point around 2007, but we think that point is an outlier.
We wonder who the marathoners are and what sports they played when they were younger? Did they do track and field?
What impact does this topic have on you and your community? This topic shows me that women are getting faster and faster which means they are probably breaking records and pushing their bodies harder than ever before. raw_comment: We noticed that the average time of the marathoners has consistently decreased, when taking away the outliers. This leads us to believe that the average marathoner has gotten faster over time. We wonder how the marathoners have decreased their times of the years? Are they training differently in order to increase their endurance and stamina? Are they training more or less than before? Is it possible that the advancement in shoe technology has led to the drop in time? Is it possible that they are just healthier overall? 2005-06 seems to have some of the slowest times in the past 20 years, but it also has the fastest singular time. How so, and why is that one time so much quicker than the rest of the times from that year? This topic can impact our community by encouraging people to train and work towards their goals The slowest times each year have gotten faster, but the fastest time from each year don't have any real pattern. In most years, there also seems to be one time/runner who is significantly faster than the rest. Also, the fastest time each year seems to be somewhat consistent every year, hovering around the 2:20:00 to 2:25:00 range. Our title is "Runners work their socks off to get better".

You can also see that the plots are close together, mostly in clumps. However, as you look at the top of the graph, where the fastest times are located, you can see how spread out they are. I notice that in the graph there is a steady upwards trend which means that the women are continuously getting faster. I wonder what is causing these women to get faster year after year? It also lets us know that our technology involving sports, which can include shoes, gear, and also nutrition, are helping athletes run faster times. Our title is "Female Marathoners Are Built Different: Check Out The Evidence In Their Times".

I notice how the general trend of the female marathoners are increasing in speed over the years throughout the early 2000’s to around 2020, although there are a few outliers of fast woman marathoners in the earlier years. I wonder if the general population of women marathoners are adapting to that pace of previous marathons and are running faster as a result. I don’t feel like this has such an impact of me but rather an impact in my community whereas this may influence and sway a lot of females to get involved in participating in marathons where they can work on themselves, improving their endurance and other benefits coming from running. It can show them that they can achieve any accomplishment they want breaking through the current gender bias. It could even get them somewhere farther in their life and open life changing opportunities.

raw_comment:
I notice that the graph is overall increasing in speed of running if you remove the outliers. I see that the fastest female marathoner was actually in around 2007. However, some of the slowest female marathoners were also in that year. I also see that in 2006, another year with very low and high times, there appear to be more dots.
I wonder whether there were more coaches or training methods around 2007 that caused the wide spread of marathon times. In the years following, did marathoners and their trainers find a universal method that works best for the runners? I wonder why the marathoners, once evenly dispersed with times, are moving closer together.
With runners becoming faster, the sports companies have to adjust. In my community, this means some running shoes may become more expensive because they are being made with higher quality materials. Also, people are pushing themselves in the sport of running much more, meaning that it is becoming extremely difficult to run in college or get a scholarship for this sport.
My headline for this graph would be "It Keeps You Running: The Fifty Fastest Females".

As soon as I look at the graph I notice an increase from 2000 to 2019. From 2006 to 2019 there is a huge difference in the slowest marathon finishes by women. Another thing that really sticks out to me is the outliers in the graph. For almost every year in this graph, there has been at least one woman who has finished at 2:25:00. This has an impact on the community, as when they look and see the increase of female marathoners times increase, it encourages them to strive for a goal and possibly to exceed that. Which could also result in more of an increase of times as the years go on.

raw_comment:
Right away when looking at this graph, I notice that as the years increased from 2000-2018, the speed of these women participating in marathons decreased per year. This is clear because in 2000, it appears the larger majority of women fell in between 2:45:00 and 2:35:00 whereas in 2018 the large majority of numbers fell in between 2:35:00 and 2:25:00. In comparing these times, I wonder what is the varying age group of these women, what kind of shape are these women in? All of these factors come into play when comparing these numbers. I can infer that as the years went on, training for marathons became more common and available which might be a reason why numbers roughly decreased. Although this does not have an impact on me because I am not a runner, it does impact runners in community looking to make a career out of this exercise. This is because as times decrease, running must be becoming more competitive. 
Headline: Women are Making Big Strides Towards Becoming Faster and Greatly Decreasing Their Marathon Times!

raw_comment:
I notice that the times of the 50 fastest women’s marathons have gradually decreased as the years go on from 2000 to 2008. With a few exceptions scattered among the years, namely 2002 and 2006, the graph shows an upward linear trendline. However, because the y-axis is formatted in decreasing order from bottom to top, the upward trend indicates a downward trend in marathon times. I wonder how this data was collected. How did the source verify that the times they collected were really the fastest times in the country? Did their sample size include every single female marathon runner in the U.S.? The data in the graph has an impact on my peers who are looking to be recruited by colleges for the upcoming year. As times become faster, it is harder to distinguish yourself from other runners, making it more difficult to get recruited.

One effect this graph has on my community is motivation towards training.  I believe that a lot of people in my fairly rural area have put together running groups to support each other.  Online resources help to connect local runners, as well as provide running and dietary plans.

raw_comment:
1. In the graph, I noticed that there have been consistently more and more female marathon runners, especially in the last twenty years. In addition, as I viewed the graph I noticed that the fastest times for said marathons have--for lack of a better phrase--decreased and gotten significantly better as time has increased. The average time in 2020 was about 2:45:00 while the average time in 2018 was closer to 2:25:00.

2. As I viewed this graph I wondered why there had been such a drastic change of both the marathon time and the amount of women running marathons in the last twenty years. I also wonder if the decrease in marathon time has any direct correlation to the increase of women's health?

3. Finally, I would like to share my title for this graph as I think it is relatively catchy: Look Out World: Women's Marathon Times are Decreasing!

Today’s graph shows the times of the 50 fastest U.S. women marathoners for the years 2000 - 2020.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in the graph. 

On Thursday afternoon, we’ll reveal the article that included these visual representations and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”

raw_comment:
3. The data not only impacts my community through motivation, but it motivates me to thrive and push myself to the limits. A positive mindset is always necessary to have when doing any physical activity, and for running the worst thing to happen is when an individual loses morale. The scatterplot of the improving times can motivate anyone to put a positive mindset on all activities and to try to push a little harder every time. The graph also motivates me to push harder in all the activities I do. Recently I have been running and enjoying the gorgeous weather, and the scatterplot influences me to push harder and try to stretch the distance a little more each time. 

4. The scatter plot is showing a positive correlation between years and the improvement of time per mile. As the years' progress, the shorter and more improved the times are. If I were to write an intriguing headline, I would title the graph, "Sustaining the Stamina". I would name the graph that because as the years go by, the runners improve their time per mile, and with running, longer stamina can stretch the energy of a runner.

raw_comment:
In the graph, the mean time for completion has increased by over 10 minutes. More notably, the gap of talent between the slowest and fastest runners has nearly halved from around 25 to 13 minutes. However, the peak times have not increased. The increase in average times is likely due to increased talent scouting and selection (pooling competitors from more countries, cities, etc) as well as a greater understanding of running biomechanics and training modalities. On the other hand, the top runner is roughly consistent with finishing times - meaning that shattering the previously conceived maximum human potential is very difficult. Genetically, these Women have not evolved - but the  level of competition in the event has. 
This is a shared phenomenon among many sports when the level of human potential is questioned. For example, the average baseball pitch is roughly 10 miles-per-hour faster than it was 20 years ago due to increased training and scouting, but the fastest pitch thrown in history has not changed since 1974.

raw_comment:
1. The average running speed of the top 50 women marathoners has increased since 2000 (since the average time taken to run the marathon has decreased). This seems to particularly be due to an increase towards the bottom of the spread on the graph.
2. I can think of some potential causes of this, with the broad overview being an increase in the number of women running marathons overtime. Now, with a growing population, that seems obvious, but I wonder if the rate of change in the running speed might be affected by certain factors relating to women's sports in particular. For example, if most women who would be achieving top marathon times would be in their 20s, did the average speed of women running marathons increase faster than usual during the 90s, when the first generations affected by Title IX and the increasing gender parity in school sports reached that age? How does this correlate with standards of living in general? And what do the averages look like for all women finishing marathons?
3. It is certainly heartening to see that athletes are getting fitter over time, though I can't say what this means for gender equality without comparing it to the times for men. Broadly speaking, it's a positive trend.
4. "Top Women Runners Getting Faster" (I tried to be catchy without getting less accurate, but it is a bit vague; I don't know how to make the word "marathon" catchy).

raw_comment:
Women, without doubt, have become more agile when running marathons in the past 20 years. At the start of the century, their range was between 2:47:00 and 2:27:00. Now, their times have dropped to around 2:35:00 through 2:22:00. That means that their maximum time has decreased by nearly 12 minutes and their minimum by 5 minutes. Furthermore, the female's times have become more spread out. Meaning, the dots on the graph have become more dispersed, instead of being concentrated at the maximum times. One other trend I observed is that there were fewer runners recorded in the past couple years. I did some tedious counting and found out that around the start of the graph, there were about 70 athletes, but in the more recent years, about 40 athletes have competed. In summary, women have improved their times for running marathons, however they also have grown to be fewer and farther between. 

I wonder if this tendency also applies to men?

This perseverance and dedication proves to me that it is possible to improve anything, even when I may think it is already flawless.

My graph's headline would be: "Catch Me if You Ever Can".

raw_comment:
Women, without doubt, have become more agile when running marathons in the past 20 years. At the start of the century, their range was between 2:47:00 and 2:27:00. Now, their times have dropped to around 2:35:00 through 2:22:00. That means that their maximum time has decreased by nearly 12 minutes and their minimum by 5 minutes. Furthermore, the female's times have become more spread out. Meaning, the dots on the graph have become more dispersed, instead of being concentrated at the maximum times. One other trend I observed is that there were fewer runners recorded in the past couple years. I did some tedious counting and found out that around the start of the graph, there were about 70 athletes, but in the more recent years, about 40 athletes have competed. In summary, women have improved their times for running marathons, however they also have grown to be fewer and farther between. 

I wonder if this tendency also applies to men?

This perseverance and dedication proves to me that it is possible to improve anything, even when I may think it is already flawless.

My graph's headline would be: "Catch Me if You Ever Can".

raw_comment:
1. There's an upward trend in women's top marathon times over the past two decades. The average top time each year seems to be getting smaller (meaning the runners are getting faster). 

2. I wonder why the outlier times (the very fastest 2-3 times each year) don't follow a similar trend as the average. And what could be causing the increase in the general population, that isn't reflected in the very top runners? 

I'm also curious about which dots represent the same women, and what other information could be gleaned if you looked at the trajectories of individual women over time. I'm interested in whether each dot represents a distinct woman or a distinct time (i.e. could the same woman be responsible for multiple dots in the same year?)

I also wonder what this same graph would look like with the 50 fastest men's marathons. 

3. This suggests something to me about women's achievement in athletics (we keep getting better and better over time!) and makes me excited about the future of women athletes. Growth is achievable, and the graph encourages me to have patience with myself and my communities, because these marathoners' growth occurred over decades.

4. Long distance, long-term: a look at the fastest women marathoners of the 21st century

raw_comment: Between 2000 to 2019, the 50 fastest women marathoners have unquestionably increased their speed (decreasing their finish time). If you drew a line along the bottom of the graph, it would be a linear, increasing line. The line would start near 2:45:00 in 2000 and end near 2:35:00 in 2019. Which means, the runners decreased their finish time by approximately 10 minutes between those years. There are many outliers near 2:20:00 and the faster times. Specifically at 2012, you can see a major gap between 2:45:00 and about 2:37:00. There were no times above 2:37:00 for 2012. I wonder what occurred that year that created a significant difference in finish times. What did the runners do in preparation to peak in that year? Personally, viewing this graph is inspirational. This shows a major achievement for women and their extreme dedication and resilience. It is incredible that these women have continued to participate in marathons throughout 19 years. That is unbelievable perseverance and commitment. The traits that these women have are some that I value in my own life and wish to develop for the future. Everyone should use this as an example in their life and think about these individuals when things become difficult. A headline that relates to the graph is "Fast Times for Long Distances".
